Every order used to be a long WhatsApp thread. 💬

Price lists, stock checks, shipping quotes per city, matching bank-transfer screenshots… all by hand. For a small florist, that means missed orders and lost custom requests.
So I built Pinkara Studio a real online flower shop. 🌸

From browsing to delivery, everything now runs in one place:
→ Mobile-first storefront with variants & add-ons
→ Live JNE / J&T shipping rates across Indonesia
→ QRIS & virtual account payments with a live countdown
→ Order tracking, cancellations & refunds
→ Custom bouquets: brief → chat → quote → pay in one click
→ An admin dashboard so the owner never misses an order

But the part I'm most proud of is what you don't see.

E-commerce gets messy when things happen at the same time:
• Double-click "Place order"? Still just one order.
• 8 buyers grabbing the last item? Only 1 wins, and stock never goes negative.
• "First 5 buyers" promo? Exactly 5, even under load.
• Payment arrives at the last second? No clash with the expiry job.

Money and stock have to stay correct, always.

Strategic Thinking Series
DON'T FOLLOW THE CURRENT. DECIDE WHERE IT FLOWS.
SICS Expo 2026: A Celebration of Learning, Sharing, & Growing Together with Farmers
...

November 7, 2026 | Banjaratma village, Brebes, Central Java, Indonesia.
It was more than an exhibition. It was a celebration of learning, sharing, & togetherness.

Our deepest appreciation to the Regent of Brebes, Mrs. Hj. Paramitha Widya Kusuma, S.E., M.M., for joining 1,500 farmers & officially inaugurating SICS Expo 2026. Her presence meant more than a formal ceremony. There is something profoundly meaningful when a leader steps down, comes closer to the people.

Brebes is not just a spot on the map. It is the heartland of Indonesia's shallot industry. Its soil tells farmers' stories of hard work, perseverance, & courage.

FROM EXHIBITION TO CELEBRATION

Many expos resemble night markets: bright lights attract attention, but do not always leave lasting meaning. SICS Expo 2026 aspired to go beyond that. Not merely displaying products, but demonstrating real evidence. Products may promise hope, but only tangible results build conviction.

In Banjaratma, farmers do not judge crops by attractive labels. They read the leaves, observe the roots, & measure the harvest. Our advice moved beyond a formula on paper, becoming an integrated living solution where nutrition, crop protection, agronomy, & data meet in the field.

FROM SELLERS TO TRUSTED FRIENDS

Our field force is not there merely to deliver products & chase transactions. They are trusted agronomic advisors & problem solvers. 
Trust is like a root. It grows quietly, requiring time, patience, & sincerity. It cannot be forced through promotion, let alone purchased with discounts.

Behind every farmer stands a family, children's education, & a future entrusted to every season. Algorithms may read numbers, but only a well-trained heart can understand the worries hidden behind a farmer's eyes.

DON'T FOLLOW THE CURRENT. DECIDE WHERE IT FLOWS.

A river that simply follows the current will eventually reach the same destination. But those brave enough to shape its direction can create new streams & discover sources of life others have yet to reach.

That is how strategy should work. Do not merely react to market changes. Learn to recognize the early signals before they become overwhelming currents.
In Banjaratma, we brought Santani Sales War Room (SSWR) into the market heartbeat. Reading farmers' behavior, distribution dynamics, competitors' movements, & hidden opportunities behind every shift.

SICS Expo 2026 reminded us that technology is not the final destination. It creates attraction, solutions deliver value, People drive competitive advantage, & Leadership safeguards direction & consistency.

And trust? It is never something we can demand from farmers. It is the harvest of a long journey where promises, proof, & sincerity grow together.

The piece is titled "Indonesia–Singapore Relations: The High Cost of Impulsive Diplomacy", which was published on November 18, 2026, in the RSIS Commentaries by the RSIS | S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies.

In this article, we discuss how the future of Indonesia–Singapore relations may be jeopardised by a pattern of impulsive diplomacy, particularly under the Prabowo Subianto administration. We argue that such an approach could undermine decades of fruitful cooperation, trade, and investment between the two nations. The article examines how President Prabowo’s tendency to react swiftly and blame external actors, rather than address underlying domestic challenges, risks damaging trust and mutual benefit between the two countries.

We also highlight broader implications for Indonesia, including the risk of neglecting pressing issues like forest and land fires, which require sustained, collaborative solutions. Our piece ultimately calls for a more measured, strategic approach to foreign policy to protect Indonesia’s national interests and maintain strong regional partnerships.

COP31 Türkiye, Day 4 – Antalya  

Disinformation is a story, not just a wrong fact. I started the day at the PRAXIS project launch on societal resilience in an age of climate disinformation. In a hands-on exercise, we compared how wildfires in Türkiye, the UK, and Brazil get blamed on developers, politicians, or NGOs. I shared Australia's version. The panellists Rabia Karakaya Polat, Seda Demiralp, Thiago S. Gouvêa Lago Dominguez Teles, and Silvia Maria Manfredi made the key point: disinformation functions as a narrative with villains, victims, and someone to blame. Their evidence shows that how easily people fall for disinformation has little to do with politics and a lot to do with how well they cope with uncertainty. 

AtEvidence for Climate Action (E4CA), Sven Harten moderated a sharp panel, and the message was to start from the decision you want to inform, not from the research question. I asked how academics can get involved, and it was great to receive helpful information from all the panellists and a chat with Sven afterwards.

Blue carbon is far more complicated than I had thought. The ASEAN Pavilion session on financing ASEAN's blue economy showed how many threads have to come together for a mangrove project. You need comprehensive, measurable ecological data and clear land rights for coastal communities that own the land. The project also has to earn international recognition for its carbon credits and deliver real financial return for investors, with Indonesia's new regulation aiming to make communities shareholders rather than just landowners who are paid rent. 

At Innovating Finance and disability inclusive climate action at the Australia Pavilion,Sainimili Tawake of the Pacific Disability Forum said people with disabilities are not passive recipients but architects of adaptation. The speakers also called for "15% for 15%: putting 15% of budgets toward inclusion, matching the share of people living with disability. The practical example of early warnings for disability is also impressive.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗖𝗹𝗼𝘂𝗱 𝗚𝗲𝘁𝘀 𝗮 𝗖𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗺𝘀 𝗗𝗲𝘀𝗸 ☁️

Washington no longer treats AI chips only as goods that cross borders. Rented computing power now crosses them too.

A new US export rule, released this week and effective on Federal Register publication, does two things. First, it requires a licence to supply advanced chips to any data centre, anywhere, giving companies parented in China or other countries of concern more than 12 million TPP of processing performance. Our arithmetic: roughly 760 H100-class chips, counted across linked sites. Second, it requires a licence for advanced chips to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand, flagged as higher-than-normal diversion risks.

📌 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗹 𝗱𝗲𝘁𝗮𝗶𝗹
Recipients with a US headquarters or US ultimate parent skip the licence if the exporter files monthly reports. Everyone else applies case by case. In five fast-growing data-centre markets, the cost of adding capacity now depends on the nationality of the operator's parent.

⚙️ 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗺𝗲𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗶𝘀𝗺
1️⃣ The data centre becomes the checkpoint. Operators must run ownership and control checks on tenants. A provider that will not share them is presumed to give the supplier knowledge of a problem.
2️⃣ Compute capacity becomes licensable. Facilities already serving covered tenants have 90 days to obtain a licence.
3️⃣ Competitive asymmetry is built in. US-parented buyers get a reporting route; local, Gulf, European and Asian operators get licence queues.
4️⃣ Host governments are on notice. Commerce may answer tolerated evasion with downgrades, Entity List additions or wider restrictions.

🎯 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗼 𝗱𝗼 𝗻𝗼𝘄
▪️ Renting GPU capacity in these markets? Ask your provider how it will source new chips and what ownership data it will need from you.
▪️ If your group has a Chinese shareholder or ultimate parent, audit every compute contract for change-of-use and termination triggers.
▪️ Developers and lenders: stress-test build-outs for licence delays and tenant mix.
▪️ Governments courting AI investment: enforcement capacity is now part of the pitch.

🔭 𝗢𝘂𝗿 𝘃𝗶𝗲𝘄
This rule converts chip leverage into leverage over who may rent compute, and where. Johor, Singapore, Jakarta and São Paulo have sold power, land and neutrality. Now compliance credibility with Washington sets their growth ceiling. Expect US clouds to gain share there, and a parallel non-US compute stack to deepen elsewhere.

Sharing an interesting article from DW on Megaspeed.

It explains that Megaspeed is what is known as a "neocloud" -- a company which buys chips and computing power and rents them out to other companies. Megaspeed's largest client, for example, is Alibaba. 

US export controls generally prohibit high-performance chips like the ones Nvidia produces from being sold to Chinese end users. They have, however, historically tolerated data centers with such chips being rented out to Chinese companies, which has allowed Chinese AI developers to train models in chips without the chips ever reaching China. 

Furthermore, in December 2025, Bloomberg reported Megaspeed had become Nvidia's largest buyer in southeast Asia, prompting concerns the company was smuggling the chips themselves to China. 

Within the past few days, the Department of Commerce -- at the behest of the Treasury Department and National Security Council -- has attempted to close this loophole. They will now require companies to apply for a license before selling advanced AI-capable chips to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil -- countries deemed at higher risk of diversion to China. This will allow Commerce to make a decision in a case-by-case basis whether to allow the sales to proceed.

Learning to see beyond the surface
 
I recently finished Belajar Fundamental Deep Learning at Dicoding through the Asah program. It's a 110-hour class with 9 modules, and Dicoding is a Google Developers Authorized Training Partner, so the material follows industry standards.  

The class started with how deep learning works and how to build and train neural networks with TensorFlow and Keras. From there it moved into real use cases. For natural language processing, I worked with text processing and built models for tasks like text classification and sentiment analysis. For time series, I learned LSTM and RNN. For image classification, I covered preprocessing, training, and evaluating the model.  

What I enjoyed most was seeing how many different problems one approach can solve. Text, sequences, and images all need different handling, but the logic behind them connects. The class also covered recommendation systems, reinforcement learning with Markov Model and Q-learning, and generative AI, which showed me how far this field goes beyond what I expected.  

One module I found especially useful was about converting machine learning models, which covers how to deploy a model to different platforms and environments. Before this, I only thought about training a model. Now I also think about how it actually gets used.  

The class ended with a final project: building a deep learning model that classifies images. Putting preprocessing, training, and evaluation together in one project made everything click.  

I'm still at the beginning, but now I understand how deep learning works in practice, and I'm excited to explore it further.

From zero to building ML models
 
Last month I finished Belajar Machine Learning untuk Pemula at Dicoding through the Asah program. It's a 90-hour class across 8 modules, and Dicoding is a Google Developers Authorized Training Partner, so the material follows current industry standards.

The first modules covered what ML actually is, and the full workflow of a project: collecting data, building a model, evaluating it, and getting it ready to use. After that, I started building. I trained classification models with K-Nearest Neighbors and Decision Tree, used linear regression to predict continuous values, and used K-Means to group data that had no labels at all. Watching an algorithm find clusters on its own was my favorite part.

The later modules were the ones that changed how I think. Feature engineering showed me that better input often beats a fancier algorithm. Overfitting and underfitting explained why a model can look great during training and still fail on new data. And hyperparameter tuning taught me how to squeeze better accuracy out of a model I thought was already done.

The class ended with a final project: building supervised and unsupervised learning models on a real-world tabular dataset, from start to finish. That's where all the separate modules finally connected.

I'm still at the beginning of this journey, but now I know how an ML project is put together, and I'm excited to try it on problems I care about.

The U.S. Commerce Department released an interim rule on Monday requiring data centers in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia to obtain a U.S. government license to buy advanced AI chips, including those from NVIDIA. The rule targets the region's role in supplying computing power to Chinese companies and puts pressure on a fast-growing data center market.

• Facilities already serving large Chinese customers have 90 days to apply for a license or face future export restrictions
• U.S.-linked firms are exempt, leaving a narrow route for Chinese companies to keep renting advanced computing power through American cloud providers
• U.S. restrictions on Nvidia's most advanced chips pushed Chinese firms, including Alibaba Group and ByteDance, to rent capacity in overseas data centers
• About 75% of China's overseas AI compute was forecast to sit in Southeast Asia by the end of 2026
• Analysts expect building and operating data centers in the region to become slower and costlier, with possible pressure on the business model of neoclouds
• Malaysia has the highest exposure: more than half of its data center capacity sits in colocation facilities, with Chinese firms accounting for a sizeable share of workloads, and large capacity is being built in Johor
• One analysis estimates the rule could cut 0.2 percentage points from Malaysia's GDP growth forecasts through 2028
• Thailand has more than 60 data centers operating and about 30 under construction. Its vice minister for commerce said the country will crack down on facilities that re-export chips to third countries, and new projects without U.S. approval may not complete construction
• Malaysia's investment, trade and industry minister said operators must follow U.S. regulations to stay in the game
• Singapore plans to negotiate trusted access to advanced AI chips for its companies
• Some high-end capacity may shift to Japan, South Korea and Taiwan, though power and land constraints may limit absorption
• Chinese developer Moonshot AI has tried to access Nvidia chips through data centers in Europe
• Oracle canceled a multibillion-dollar chip-leasing agreement with Tencent in early November that would have given Tencent access to about 100,000 advanced AI chips
• One analyst warned Chinese companies could pivot from renting compute in Southeast Asia to renting from data centers in Virginia

Export controls are now shaping where AI data center capacity gets built and who can use it.

My first step into Python
 
I recently finished Memulai Pemrograman dengan Python at Dicoding through the Asah program. It's a 60-hour class with 12 modules, and Dicoding is a Google Developers Authorized Training Partner, so the material follows industry standards.  

The early modules were about the basics: writing my first code, working with different kinds of data, then expressions and sequential actions. Once I got comfortable there, control flow opened up a lot. Conditions, loops, and error handling are what make a program actually do something instead of just running top to bottom.  

After that came arrays, matrices, and subprograms. Splitting a big problem into small functions was the point where coding started to feel less like memorizing and more like problem solving. I also went through object-oriented programming, with classes, methods, attributes, and inheritance. That one took a few tries before it made sense.  

The modules I didn't expect to care about were style guide and unit testing. Learning PEP8 made me pay attention to how my code reads, and unit testing taught me to check that my code really does what I think it does. Before that, "it runs" was my only standard.  

The class closed with popular libraries for data processing, web scraping, and even machine learning, which got me curious about what to learn next. Then a final exam, and the certificate.  

Now I have a solid base in Python and the confidence to keep building on it.  

Thank you Dicoding Indonesia andGoTo Group for the Asah program.

Buildings account for around 30–40% of Indonesia’s energy use and in many building types cooling alone makes up more than 60% of that.

Plenty of efficiency measures pay back quickly, but while the investment comes upfront, the savings arrive over years and lending typically hasn’t been structured around that.

On Monday, 16 November 2026, Indonesia’s Financial Services Authority (OJK) launched its Green Building Sustainability-Linked Loan Guideline. OJK developed the guideline with the Green Finance Institute Indonesia and the Global Buildings Performance Network (GBPN), with support from the UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office.

The guideline focuses on how banks, developers and building owners can utilise sustainability-linked loans for green buildings. With these loans, the borrower pays a lower margin when the building meets agreed, independently verified targets for energy, emissions or water.

The guideline brings engineering and finance together, covering:

- The targets lenders can use
- How to phase a retrofit so early savings help fund the next stage
- How results are verified
- How to build a business case a bank can assess.

It follows a series of forums with regulators, banks and developers, and it gives each new deal a shared starting point instead of a blank page.

As Poppy Ismalina, Country Director of GFI Indonesia, puts it: “Our objective with this guideline is to make cost-efficient green building investments bankable at scale, by aligning technical measures with financial incentives that work for both banks and developers. This will be followed by hands-on capacity building to ensure the guideline is applied in practice.”

𝗔𝗜 𝗡𝗘𝗘𝗗𝗦 𝗪𝗔𝗧𝗘𝗥. 𝗦𝗢 𝗗𝗢 𝗣𝗘𝗢𝗣𝗟𝗘.
Data centres are powering Southeast Asia’s AI ambitions. But are we planning for the communities living alongside them?

The region is competing for billions in data-centre investment. Governments see foreign investment, jobs, technology and a stronger position in the global AI economy.

But what does this mean for local communities?

In Batam, residents have protested over serious water shortages. Some believe nearby data-centre expansion is contributing.

Authorities have attributed the shortages to drought and infrastructure problems, and a direct link to data centres has not been established. Nevertheless, BP Batam has required investors to develop their own water supplies, including desalination facilities.

And this isn’t just Indonesia.

In Kota Damansara, Malaysia, a proposed data-centre development was withdrawn following local opposition and a petition attracting more than 9,000 signatures.

Johor’s rapid growth as a data-centre hub is also bringing scrutiny over water, electricity and environmental impact.

Just days ago, Malaysia’s Queen called for careful assessment of data centres’ impact on resources and local communities.

I don’t believe we should stop building data centres. Far from it.

AI and digital infrastructure represent enormous opportunities for Southeast Asia. We need investment, innovation and the industries that will support future growth.

But attracting investment is only part of the equation.

𝗛𝗢𝗪 𝗗𝗢 𝗪𝗘 𝗧𝗨𝗥𝗡 𝗧𝗛𝗔𝗧 𝗜𝗡𝗩𝗘𝗦𝗧𝗠𝗘𝗡𝗧 𝗜𝗡𝗧𝗢 𝗦𝗨𝗦𝗧𝗔𝗜𝗡𝗔𝗕𝗟𝗘 𝗘𝗖𝗢𝗡𝗢𝗠𝗜𝗖 𝗔𝗡𝗗 𝗦𝗢𝗖𝗜𝗔𝗟 𝗩𝗔𝗟𝗨𝗘?

Where will the water and electricity come from? What happens during drought or pressure on the power grid?

Will local people get jobs and training? Will local businesses benefit? Are communities consulted before decisions are made, or only after plans are approved?

This brings me to something businesses sometimes overlook: 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝗼𝗰𝗶𝗮𝗹 𝗹𝗶𝗰𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝘁𝗼 𝗼𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲.

Planning approval gives a company the legal right to build. It doesn’t automatically earn the trust of the people living next door.

That has to be earned through transparency, credible evidence, consultation and action.

Southeast Asia has a huge opportunity to become a major hub for AI and digital infrastructure.

𝗟𝗲𝘁’𝘀 𝗴𝗲𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗱𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹𝗼𝗽𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗿𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁, 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗷𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗶𝗻𝘃𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗻𝘂𝗺𝗯𝗲𝗿𝘀.

I first met #CPT (the Climate Predictability Tool) briefly as an undergraduate. I only started using it seriously during the 2015#ElNiño, while working on a fire risk system for Indonesia. In 2023, I came back to it through #PyCPT, its #Python interface.

CPT comes with detailed help pages, and the IRI team publishes PyCPT notebooks and training material. That is how I learned to run it. What I wanted to add is a companion to those: the same steps followed through on one country, on real data, all the way to a forecast you can check against what happened.

So I wrote one, as a casual weekend project. PyCPT Tutorial is now online:https://lnkd.in/gVhvP__F

It was built with PyCPT 2.10.4 and CPT 17.8.3.

What is inside:
- Twelve worked cases, all forecasting rainfall over Indonesia and all verified against 2023
- Five time scales: seasonal, monthly, dekad, weekly and pentad
- Each time scale done twice: with one model, and with a multi-model ensemble
- #CHIRPS v3.0 as the observations, at 0.05 degree, summarized for 38 provinces
- A seven-chapter “Learn PyCPT” track: getting the data, bringing your own observations, evaluating a model, reading probabilistic forecasts, combining models and adapting it to your region
- Every case is an executed notebook with its outputs saved, so you can read it in the browser or rerun it yourself

It also shows the results that surprised me. One example: at subseasonal scales, calibrating five models and averaging them barely improved on calibrating a single model, and the plain average of the raw models correlated better with observations than any calibrated forecast, at every lead I tested. The tutorial shows that result as it is and does not claim to explain it.

Skill also drops quickly with lead time, and the pages show that too. Knowing where a forecast stops being useful is part of forecasting.

This is a learning resource, not a replacement for the official CPT and PyCPT documentation. The source is open (MPL 2.0):https://lnkd.in/gCDaNP2e

Credit to the International Research Institute for Climate and Society (IRI) team behind CPT and PyCPT, to the modeling centers whose forecasts are served through the IRI Data Library, and to the CHIRPS team at the Climate Hazards Center. This tutorial is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or maintained by the IRI or the developers of PyCPT and CPT.

If you work on seasonal or subseasonal forecasting and find something wrong or unclear, please open an issue. Corrections are welcome.

The weirdest job rejection reason I have seen.

A qualified candidate in Sweden just received this exact reply from a hiring team:

"It's quite strange that you only identify yourself by just one name. This does not give us the confidence we need to continue reviewing your expression of interest."

Not a lack of skills. Not a failed interview. Just a missing surname.

Across India, Indonesia, and Afghanistan, millions of people legally have a single name. Yet in parts of the Western world, something as ordinary as a one-word name is still treated like a red flag.

I know this firsthand. Because my legal name is just "Kush," my own official company record once had to be filed as "Kush LNU" (Last Name Unknown) just to get past a two-box form.

A form failing on one name is a software bug. A recruiter saying one name "does not give us the confidence" to consider a candidate is Discrimination.

Even Stockholm University’s research found that immigrants in Sweden who changed foreign-sounding surnames to Swedish ones saw their annual earnings jump by 141%—proving how deeply name discrimination still operates beneath the surface.
Sweden is rightly admired worldwide for its inclusiveness and policy leadership. A handful of gatekeepers with outdated assumptions shouldn't undermine the fairness the country stands for.

What is the most arbitrary reason you have ever seen a qualified candidate get rejected for?

I have just encounter the company that are quite unethical and unprofessional. I think can be one of the worst so far that I have come across with and it is a Singapore base company...

1. No offer letter to the newly recruit (Malaysian, Myanmar, Indonesian and others)
2. Some of the employees recruit to work from home but there is no compensation on anything. Meaning the employee needs to use their own laptop, electricity and wifi from home. 
3. They are required to work 9 hours a day (6am - 3pm, 9am-6pm and 1pm-10pm) with one hour break. They need to report when they are on lunch or toilet break. They are expected to turn on their zoom to prove they are working and if any inquiry come in with no one replying then they would be interrogate of their whereabout. 
4. Most of the staff are recruited at around SGD400 - SGD600 without any CPF contribution at their home country. 
5. The staff is required to sell property but without any commission. If they wanted to earn commission, they need to sell at least 45 houses in 3 months. 
6. Once there are annual dinner held in Johor. Most of the staff from KL are required to drive down and then make it a day trip because company does not arrange any hotel arrangement. 
7. First 3 days of working does not have any salary because the company is conducting training and sharing knowledge. The first paid day counted after the 3 days training. 

Honestly, there are so many red flags because even hiring a Singaporean base employee without any experience (fresh graduate) it is around SGD3000 and above. That is not counted the CPF, Leaves, Medical, Office Rental, Laptop and other necessary tools and equipment. Yes I understand they are hiring someone base in Malaysia, Indonesia or Myanmar where their home country salary base is low but to suppress and treating others in such way is just inappropriate.

Are we becoming too old to be employable in Indonesia's job market?

There's something I've been thinking about lately.

Being in your 30s in Indonesia's job market can feel like you're already an expired product.

You're sometimes considered too experienced for a Specialist position, but not senior enough for a Manager position.

Companies want someone with 7–10 years of experience, strong problem-solving skills, stakeholder management capabilities, and the ability to work independently.

But when it comes to salary expectations, suddenly your experience becomes a concern.
Isn't that ironic?

I understand that hiring decisions involve many factors, including business needs, budgets, and organizational structures.

But I think we need to reconsider how we evaluate experienced professionals.

Being 30+ doesn't mean someone is less adaptable, less ambitious, or less willing to learn.

Some are changing careers. Some are rebuilding after unexpected setbacks. 

Some are simply looking for a workplace where their experience can make a difference.

And none of those things should automatically make them less employable.

Your professional value shouldn't come with an expiration date.

I'd genuinely love to hear from recruiters, hiring managers, and fellow professionals:

Have you ever felt that age became an invisible barrier in your career?

posts.text:
I’ve been having a lot of conversations recently about navigating diverse APAC markets and the importance of localisation. And by recently, I mean for the last nine years since I arrived in Singapore.

My own cultural wake up call came right at the start of my Singapore adventure and it was a tough one.

I'd rocked up in Singapore – single and poor – on a one-way ticket hoping to land a job quickly. But I soon discovered that it was just before CNY when many companies slow their hiring processes. I struggled to even get interviews but eventually hustled enough to find work just before my legal, financial and mental runway fell off a cliff. 

Quick pause here for my Singaporean and expat contacts to do a mini-eyeroll as they’ll consider this level of cultural understanding to be table stakes – like listing ChatGPT on your CV. And they’re completely right. But it’s surprising how many overseas companies get this spectacularly wrong.

People still bucket APAC markets together and presume that whatever works at HQ will translate over here. But there's no one-size-fits-all approach – there isn’t even a matching pair of shoes. Every market is different, with its own languages, religions, customs, business practices and more.

Take the humble business card as an example. 

In China you should hand a card to the most senior person first. 

In Japan, exchanging 'meishi' can be a formal ritual where you treat the card like a valued object.

In Indonesia it’s disrespectful to pass a card with just your left hand. 

And that’s just scratching the surface. As an APAC representative you need to be acutely aware of these subtle differences but also try to learn as much as possible from your regional teams. 

A former manager in the US told me he completely trusted my APAC expertise and would take direction from me instead of the other way around (incidentally that same manager flew to Japan to fire someone in person instead of doing the dirty over a call so the employee could save face – cultural champ move right there).

So when I was planning my agency Reverb Marketing six years ago, I kitchen sinked everything from my career: digital marketing, comms, copywriting, events, demand gen, CRM, personal branding, influencers and a whole lot more.    

But then I took a step back and realised that my biggest superpower wasn’t any of those hard-earned skills. It was simply being on the ground in Singapore and recognising the complexities of the region.

Understanding the nuances. 

Having a pulse on the landscape. 

Accepting there'll always be cultural curveballs.

And it’s a crucial skill to have – one that we probably take for granted here because it’s become so ingrained in us.

Every day's a cultural school day in this incredible part of the world and I’m sure there are plenty more mistakes waiting to happen. Have you ever made a cultural faux pas? Share in the comments! 

–

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗖𝗹𝗼𝘂𝗱 𝗚𝗲𝘁𝘀 𝗮 𝗖𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗺𝘀 𝗗𝗲𝘀𝗸 ☁️

Washington no longer treats AI chips only as goods that cross borders. Rented computing power now crosses them too.

A new US export rule, released this week and effective on Federal Register publication, does two things. First, it requires a licence to supply advanced chips to any data centre, anywhere, giving companies parented in China or other countries of concern more than 12 million TPP of processing performance. Our arithmetic: roughly 760 H100-class chips, counted across linked sites. Second, it requires a licence for advanced chips to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand, flagged as higher-than-normal diversion risks.

📌 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗹 𝗱𝗲𝘁𝗮𝗶𝗹
Recipients with a US headquarters or US ultimate parent skip the licence if the exporter files monthly reports. Everyone else applies case by case. In five fast-growing data-centre markets, the cost of adding capacity now depends on the nationality of the operator's parent.

⚙️ 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗺𝗲𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗶𝘀𝗺
1️⃣ The data centre becomes the checkpoint. Operators must run ownership and control checks on tenants. A provider that will not share them is presumed to give the supplier knowledge of a problem.
2️⃣ Compute capacity becomes licensable. Facilities already serving covered tenants have 90 days to obtain a licence.
3️⃣ Competitive asymmetry is built in. US-parented buyers get a reporting route; local, Gulf, European and Asian operators get licence queues.
4️⃣ Host governments are on notice. Commerce may answer tolerated evasion with downgrades, Entity List additions or wider restrictions.

🎯 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗼 𝗱𝗼 𝗻𝗼𝘄
▪️ Renting GPU capacity in these markets? Ask your provider how it will source new chips and what ownership data it will need from you.
▪️ If your group has a Chinese shareholder or ultimate parent, audit every compute contract for change-of-use and termination triggers.
▪️ Developers and lenders: stress-test build-outs for licence delays and tenant mix.
▪️ Governments courting AI investment: enforcement capacity is now part of the pitch.

🔭 𝗢𝘂𝗿 𝘃𝗶𝗲𝘄
This rule converts chip leverage into leverage over who may rent compute, and where. Johor, Singapore, Jakarta and São Paulo have sold power, land and neutrality. Now compliance credibility with Washington sets their growth ceiling. Expect US clouds to gain share there, and a parallel non-US compute stack to deepen elsewhere.

Point-to-point delivers each queue message to one consumer, but that doesn't mean every consumer sees every message. When several consumers share a queue, or a consumer uses a selector, any single consumer may only get a slice of what's on the queue.

#PointToPoint #Messaging #DistributedSystems #Reliability #SystemDesign #SoftwareEngineering #BackendDevelopment #FaultTolerance #Architecture #Developers #TechCommunity #Java

More info
• In Jakarta Messaging, how messages are spread across multiple consumers on one queue isn't defined. A QueueBrowser lets you peek at queue messages without removing them, but its scan isn't required to be a static snapshot, since messages can arrive and expire while you look.

• Messages can also be delivered more than once. When a provider redelivers a message, it sets the JMSRedelivered flag to signal that it may have been delivered before, so your application should take extra care to avoid processing duplicates. The delivery count starts at 1 on first receipt and isn't guaranteed to be exact. #Idempotency #JakartaMessaging

Rule 2, outside a park: you deal directly with landowners, so due diligence decides everything. One buyer built a fence on land the land bureau said was state-owned and reserved for a dam. He lost both the investment and the asset.
